# The Space Between Things

I've been thinking about the spaces between things lately. Not the obvious gaps—the actual distance between objects sitting on a table—but the stranger, more persistent voids. The silence after someone stops talking. The pause between heartbeats. The years between childhood and now.

There's something about these in-between moments that feels more real than the things themselves.

I watched a squirrel today navigate a telephone wire. It moved with absolute certainty, never hesitating, never looking down. I wondered if it ever thinks about falling. Probably not. Probably it just knows the wire holds and that's sufficient. I've spent most of my life doubting the wire, even when it clearly holds.

My mother called this week. She asked if I'm happy, which is the kind of question that has no honest answer. You can say yes and feel like you're lying about the complexity. You can say no and sound like you're drowning. So I said something vague about things being fine, and she seemed to accept this, which made me sad for reasons I can't articulate.

There's a book on my shelf I've been meaning to read for three years. It sits there like an obligation, like a version of myself I promised I'd become. Someday I'll either read it or donate it, but the act of either seems weighted with significance it probably doesn't deserve.

I think the problem with being alive right now is that we're all pretending we know what we're doing while secretly operating from a collection of half-remembered advice and YouTube videos. We're like people trying to assemble furniture from instructions written in a language we sort of understand. And somehow it mostly holds together. Sometimes it even looks good.

The weather has been strange. Warm when it should be cold, cold when warmth would make sense. I think about climate change sometimes, then stop thinking about it because the thought is too large. It's like looking at a number with too many zeros. The human mind just bounces off it.

I went to a coffee shop yesterday and the barista spelled my name wrong, which shouldn't matter but somehow does. A small thing, a tiny assertion of my existence being mispronounced, and I felt oddly invisible. Then I wondered if that feeling means I need to be more present in the world or if it's completely normal and I'm overthinking it. (It's definitely the latter, but I'll probably worry about it for weeks.)

There's a particular anxiety that comes with entering your thirties. Not the obvious kind—the aging, the mortality, the biological clock nonsense—but something more subtle. A awareness that you're no longer becoming; you're becoming something specific now. The window is still open but it's clearly closing. Your life is no longer theoretical. It's becoming actual.

I had a friend I haven't talked to in years. We were very close once. I see his life on social media sometimes—his wedding, his children, his promotions—and I'm genuinely happy for him, but there's also this strange grief. The friendship died quietly, without drama or betrayal. We just stopped being convenient to each other, and other friendships filled the space. I think about sending him a message sometimes but I'm afraid it would be awkward. Maybe the friendship is better left as a good memory than risked as an awkward present.

This is maybe the real tragedy of adulthood: the necessary forgetting.

I tried journaling last month, thinking it would bring clarity. Instead it just filled a notebook with complaints and observations that seemed profound at 11 PM and embarrassing the next morning. I stopped after a week. Some people seem to find therapy in writing. For me it just creates evidence of how circular my thinking is.

The best part of my week is usually Wednesday mornings, which is so mundane I'm almost embarrassed to admit it. There's something about Wednesday that feels like it has potential without the pressure of Friday. Friday everyone's waiting for it. Wednesday surprises you if you're not paying attention.

I've noticed that I'm better at being a friend when I'm not trying to be one. The moment I consciously decide to reach out or remember someone's birthday because I "should," it feels obligatory and they probably sense that. But random moments of genuine thinking-about-someone seem to land differently. Maybe that's just an excuse for being flaky. Probably.

There's a weird comfort in knowing that somewhere right now, in this exact moment, someone is going through something worse than whatever I'm dealing with, and someone else is going through something better. We're all just sort of treading water at different depths in the same ocean. It's either very lonely or very connecting, depending on how you look at it.

I want to end this with something profound and neat, some tidy conclusion that brings everything together—the spaces between things, the uncertainty, the weird sadness of existence, the quiet joys of Wednesday mornings. Some sentence that suggests I've figured something out or that any of this matters.

But I don't have that. And maybe that's the point. Maybe we're all just walking around between things, trying to find meaning in the gaps, hoping the wire holds, spelling each other's names wrong, and somehow it's enough.

The squirrel made it across the telephone wire just fine. It didn't need a conclusion. It just needed to get to the other side.
